claims.claim: For the least inherently creative writers, ratings of how well the story was written rose by up to 26.6% with five AI ideas.
claims.source: Anil R. Doshi and Oliver P. Hauser, Science Advances, 12 July 2024
claims.quote: how well the story was written increase by up to 26.6%
claims.page: Results, marginal effects by DAT score

claims.claim: Among the most inherently creative writers, access to generative AI ideas had little effect on their stories' evaluations.
claims.source: Anil R. Doshi and Oliver P. Hauser, Science Advances, 12 July 2024
claims.quote: there is little effect of having access to generative AI ideas
claims.page: Results, marginal effects by DAT score

claims.claim: The generative model in the Doshi and Hauser experiment was OpenAI's GPT-4, used only to supply a three-sentence starting idea.
claims.source: Anil R. Doshi and Oliver P. Hauser, Science Advances, 12 July 2024

claims.claim: Chiang argues that when an LLM fills in the choices a prompt did not make by averaging the choices other writers made, that average amounts to the least interesting choices available, which is why AI-generated text is often bland.
claims.source: Ted Chiang, essayist and SF writer, The New Yorker, 2024
claims.quote: that average is equivalent to the least interesting choices possible
claims.page: para. beginning "If an A.I. generates a ten-thousand-word story"

claims.claim: Chiang argues that the alternative to averaging - instructing the program to mimic a specific writer's style - produces a highly derivative story rather than interesting art.
claims.source: Ted Chiang, essayist and SF writer, The New Yorker, 2024
claims.quote: which produces a highly derivative story
claims.page: para. beginning "If an A.I. generates a ten-thousand-word story"

claims.quote: the fiction generated by large language models like ChatGPT is terrible
claims.page: para. beginning "Is there anything about art"

claims.feature: other: what a human editor fixes first

claims.quote: aggressive recitation of facts with line breaks and merry affirmations

verdicts.trueWording: assessments of how well the story was written increase by up to 26.6%
verdicts.note: Europe PMC full-text XML fetched raw (HTTP 200, 98KB). Results/Heterogeneity by inherent creativity: 'For low-DAT writers in the Human with five GenAI ideas condition, assessments of how well the story was written increase by up to 26.6%'. Quote is a verbatim substring; 'low-DAT' is defined in the same paper as 'inherently less creative writers', and DAT is 'a measure of an individual's inherent creativity'. Paper's word is 'assessments', the claim says 'ratings' - same referent (third-party evaluator scores).

verdicts.trueWording: there is little effect of having access to generative AI ideas
verdicts.note: Raw XML: 'Among the most inherently creative writers (i.e., high-DAT writers), there is little effect of having access to generative AI ideas on the creativity of their stories.' Quote verbatim. The 'evaluations' limb is supported by the following sentences: 'Across all conditions, high-DAT writers' stories are evaluated relatively highly ... providing them with access to generative AI does not affect their high evaluations.'

verdicts.trueWording: OpenAI's GPT-4 LLM ... to provide a three-sentence starting idea
verdicts.note: Raw XML, study design: 'we gave writers the option to call upon a generative AI platform (OpenAI's GPT-4 LLM) to provide a three-sentence starting idea to inspire their own story writing.' Quote verbatim (curly apostrophe). The 'only' limb is corroborated in Materials and Methods: the prompt was 'Write a three-sentence summary of a story about ...', the API response was passed to the participant, and 'At the time of the study, we used the API from OpenAI's latest model, GPT-4.' The only other OpenAI call in the paper is the (non-generative) embeddings API used for the similarity analysis, so GPT-4 is indeed the sole generative model and its sole role is the starting idea.

verdicts.trueWording: that average is equivalent to the least interesting choices possible
verdicts.note: New Yorker page fetched raw with a browser UA (HTTP 200, full essay text, not a paywall stub - byline 'By Ted Chiang August 31, 2024' present). Page: 'One is to take an average of the choices that other writers have made, as represented by text found on the Internet; that average is equivalent to the least interesting choices possible, which is why A.I.-generated text is often really bland.' Quote verbatim; every limb (filling in choices the prompt did not make, averaging other writers, blandness) is on the page. Page says 'often really bland'; claim says 'often bland'.

verdicts.trueWording: which produces a highly derivative story
verdicts.note: Same paragraph: 'Another is to instruct the program to engage in style mimicry, emulating the choices made by a specific writer, which produces a highly derivative story. In neither case is it creating interesting art.' Quote verbatim; the 'rather than interesting art' limb is the next sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: Right now, the fiction generated by large language models like ChatGPT is terrible
verdicts.note: Page: 'Right now, the fiction generated by large language models like ChatGPT is terrible, but one can imagine that such programs might improve in the future.' Quote verbatim. The 'at the time of writing' limb is carried by the page's own 'Right now' and by the dateline August 31, 2024.

verdicts.trueWording: its sentences - and the small-scale choices they represent - help to determine the thriller's effectiveness
verdicts.note: Page: 'I doubt you could replace every sentence in a thriller with one that is semantically equivalent and have the resulting novel be as entertaining. This means that its sentences - and the small-scale choices they represent - help to determine the thriller's effectiveness.' Quote verbatim and both limbs present. Fidelity note for the downstream writer: Chiang hedges twice where the claim does not - 'I doubt you could' (not 'you could not') and 'help to determine' (not 'determine'). Use the page's wording if quoting.

verdicts.trueWording: it has no more intention to communicate
verdicts.note: Page: 'The fact that ChatGPT can generate coherent sentences invites us to imagine that it understands language in a way that your phone's auto-complete does not, but it has no more intention to communicate.' Quote verbatim, and the auto-complete comparison is in the same sentence. The second limb is the same paragraph's opening: 'a large language model is not a writer; it's not even a user of language. Language is, by definition, a system of communication, and it requires an intention to communicate.'

verdicts.trueWording: that is precisely what prevents them from being effective tools for artists
verdicts.note: Page: 'The selling point of generative A.I. is that these programs generate vastly more than you put into them, and that is precisely what prevents them from being effective tools for artists.' Quote verbatim, both limbs in the one sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: Google pulled the commercial after widespread backlash from viewers
verdicts.note: Page: 'Recently, Google aired a commercial during the Paris Olympics for Gemini ... The ad shows a father using Gemini to compose a fan letter, which his daughter will send to an Olympic athlete who inspires her. Google pulled the commercial after widespread backlash from viewers.' Quote verbatim; every limb (Paris Olympics, Gemini, father composing, daughter's letter, backlash, pulled) is on the page.

n+1 page fetched raw (HTTP 200, full essay, no paywall cut). Page: 'a prospect would pose a series of questions (What's the rent? And utilities? When can I move in?) and Brenda would string together a composite response that collated so much information she sounded hostile.' Quote verbatim; every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: I softened her aggressive recitation of facts with line breaks and merry affirmations
verdicts.note: Page, immediately after the composite-response sentence: 'In these cases, I softened her aggressive recitation of facts with line breaks and merry affirmations.' Quote verbatim. 'Standard intervention' is carried by the page's habitual framing ('In these cases ...', among the routine 'little collaborations' she describes).

verdicts.trueWording: Most of her missteps were errors of comprehension. She would seize on the wrong keyword and queue up a non sequitur
verdicts.note: Page: 'Most of her missteps were errors of comprehension. She would seize on the wrong keyword and queue up a non sequitur, or she would think she did not know how to answer when she actually had the right response on hand.' Quote verbatim, both limbs supported. Note the page gives a second form of the same error class (thinking she did not know an answer she had) that the claim omits; the claim does not assert exclusivity.

verdicts.trueWording: The developers touted her unrelenting consistency as a feature
verdicts.note: Page: 'Brenda's cyclical catchphrases anesthetized me into a stupor. The developers touted her unrelenting consistency as a feature. Brenda, they claimed, said the same thing to everyone, which meant that she was incapable of bias.' Quote verbatim; both limbs, including the attribution to the developers' claim, supported.

verdicts.trueWording: specifics, it turns out, were what people cared about the most
verdicts.note: Page: 'When it came to specifics, we couldn't say much, and specifics, it turns out, were what people cared about the most. Carpet or hardwood? What direction did the windows face? Of course we had no idea and neither did Brenda.' Quote verbatim; the 'neither she nor Brenda' limb is the page's 'we had no idea and neither did Brenda'.
